etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English huschen (“to hush”) (as past participle husht (“silent; hushed”) and interjection husht (“quiet!”)). Cognate with Low German huschen, hüssen (“to hush; lull”), German huschen (“to shoo; scurry”), Danish hysse (“to hush”), and maybe Albanian hesht.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To appease; to allay; to soothe.

quote.citation: 1682, Thomas Otway, Venice Preserv’d, or, A Plot Discover’d. A Tragedy. […], London:  […]  Jos[eph] Hindmarsh […], →OCLC, Act I, scene i, page 11:
quote.text: VVilt thou then / Huſh my Cares thus, and ſhelter me vvith Love?

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XIX, page 32:
quote.text: And hush’d my deepest grief of all.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To clear off soil and other materials overlying the bedrock.
A silence, especially after some noise

quote.citation: 1816, Lord Byron, “Canto III”, in Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage. Canto the Third, London: Printed for John Murray, […], →OCLC, stanza LXXXVI:
quote.text: It is the hush of night.

quote.citation: 1905, Lord Dunsany [i.e., Edward Plunkett, 18th Baron of Dunsany], The Gods of Pegāna, London: [Charles] Elkin Mathews, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: And there fell a hush upon the gods when they saw that Māna rested, and there was silence on Pegāna save for the drumming of Skarl.
